title: Conviction, Accountability and Where to Draw the Line
label: Course 2
header_line: My analysis of one book on an entrepreneur's life. Not a summary of the book. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.
outcome: My reading of one book about an entrepreneur's life, in the book's order. We look at getting lost in a goal, crisis, smart money and dumb money, where the line is, approval and accountability, and time and priorities. Built from my group calls.
season_note: A suggested run of about 26 weeks. Suggested dates only: nothing locks.

items.title: Journey: a story from me
items.idea: I ask my grandparents how they define love.

video.label: It’s just a feeling
video.transcript: I once asked my class to stop and answer one question. How do you define love? When I was in high school, I visited my grandparents. One read the paper on one side of the room, the other on the other side. Day after day, for years. One day I asked them how they define love. They laughed. It's just a feeling, they said. They felt each other's presence. That was all. They weren't overly loving people. They came from the Great Depression. So how much of that shapes us? How would you answer my grandparents' question?

items.title: Where is that line?
items.idea: Conviction versus fantasy: ask experts you admire, watch the margins, keep ego in check.

video.label: Is it conviction or fantasy?
video.transcript: How many of us could lose money for five years and still say: I'm going to make it? I'd ask a harder question. Where is the line where you say: I made a wrong call? And where is the line where you say: no, my conviction is right? I call the danger getting drunk on your own idea. You are inspired, and you stop watching the basics. Ego without logic brings you down. In my twenties I ignored the margins. Sales and volume looked great. The margins weren't there. My fix: ask people who know the field. Not an uncle in a different business. People who've done it. Write one project where you're losing money or time. Then write why you think it will work.

video.label: The possibility game
video.transcript: Say you want a company worth ten million dollars by the end of the year. Big. Scary. I say: get granular. Walk it backwards. The value you want. The sales that needs. The proposals each month. Then each week. Then each day. If we do those daily things, we are in the possibility game. If we ignore them, we're in the impossibility game. I call the daily part showing up. Visit twenty places. Send each a presentation. That's the work you control. After a while the pipeline turns into numbers. A cost to acquire a customer: your time, your money. And a formula: how do I lower it? Write one big goal. Work backwards to a day.

video.label: Approval and accountability
video.transcript: Two magic words for anyone who leads: approval and accountability. I studied a leader who makes his people want to be better. What does he do? My word: accountability. He sets goals, and he takes responsibility for them. He also reads strengths and weaknesses in everyone on his team, fast. And you never hear him say: poor me, a bigger company is bullying me. Victimizing yourself, I said, comes from a negative belief system. It's a delicate balance. Approval gives people security. Accountability makes them tough. Who do you lead? What approval do they get from you? What accountability?

video.label: The questions you ask
video.transcript: Imagine you're sitting at a table with leaders of a country in deep conflict with yours. What do you ask? My answer: suspend judgment. Listen. Be almost like a journalist, with good questions. A student's good question: what do they think the problem actually is? It's usually different from what we think it is. Will you freeze, or learn? Don't be the person who stays quiet. It works in business too. Learn who you're talking to before you decide what you think. My dialogue is determined by the questions I ask. video.label: Where did my process break down?
video.transcript: Blame feels good. For about a minute. I noticed that the leader we were studying doesn't blame anybody. Not people. Not circumstances. If you keep blaming outside things, I said, you have an inside problem. The question strong leaders ask: where did my process break down? Blame hands your power away. Auditing your process gets it back. In a small company it starts at the top. The leader takes accountability, and then everyone does. Focus on the problem. What are my options? questions.q: Is your personal life congruent with the values you talk about?
Do you honestly ask whether you are the problem?
Do you check a company's balance sheet before getting excited by its price?
Do you know what going public involves?
Can you work out your business's fundamentals in your head?

items.title: What is he repeatedly doing that is not working?
items.idea: Study whether a life is congruent with its values.

items.title: Stock doesn't necessarily mean the value of a company
items.idea: A stock price is a perception; check the fundamentals.

items.title: Anybody in the public has access to buy your company
items.idea: How a public company works, in simple terms.

items.title: Workshop: My congruence, my fundamentals
items.idea: One page, five lines.
steps: One thing I repeatedly do that is not working.
Whether my personal life is congruent with my stated values.
Something I am tempted by, and its fundamentals.
The three fundamentals of my business, in my head.
Who will read a balance sheet with me.

modules.title: What's the evidence that they care?

items.title: Check your level
items.idea: Five quick questions. They suggest where to start. Nothing locks.

questions.q: Do you know how your advisors work together?
Is your own financial reporting always honest?
Do you look for evidence of care, not just words?
Do you give your time to others?
After a big loss, do you count what you kept?

items.title: A row of bricks went up
items.idea: Watch how advisors work together; keep your numbers honest.

items.title: What's the evidence that they care?
items.idea: Look for evidence of care; study people; give your time.

items.title: He focuses on the two billion he kept
items.idea: Count what you kept; be grateful.

items.title: Workshop: My board, my evidence, my gratitude
items.idea: One page, five lines.
steps: How my advisors work together, and any wall.
The evidence that one person cares about me and my work.
What I will give: time, skills, a percent of revenue.
What I lost and what I kept.
What I am grateful for today.

modules.title: Success is a lot of tiny little decisions

items.title: Check your level
items.idea: Five quick questions. They suggest where to start. Nothing locks.

questions.q: Can you name your top three global concerns?
Is your cause part of how you present yourself?
Do you know how people describe you?
Do you know your defining moments and your tiny daily decisions?
Do you do what you talk about?

items.title: Give me your top three global concerns
items.idea: Pick a cause, make it part of who you are, and act.

items.title: The way people talk about you is your brand
items.idea: Your brand is what people say; do, don't just talk.

items.title: Success is a lot of tiny little decisions
items.idea: Look at the tiny daily decisions.

video.label: Tiny decisions
video.transcript: You don't fail because of one bad decision. I said you fail because you made small bad decisions, day after day. And success is the same. When I meet someone, I watch the habits. Do they get up in the morning? Are they structured? Do they start the day positive? Relationships work like that too. If you don't work at them every day, they drift into neglect. I also look for the defining moments in a life: a hard one, a lesson, a decision it led to. Write three defining moments. Write the emotion, the action and the decision each led to.

items.title: Get up, make the phone calls, write the letters, send the emails
items.idea: Do it: show up, be relentless.

items.title: Workshop: My cause, my brand, my daily decisions
items.idea: One page, five lines.
steps: My top three concerns and the one I will act on.
The three words I want people to use about me.
My three defining moments and what they taught me.
The tiny decision I will repeat every day this week.
Tomorrow morning's calls, letters and emails.

page_text: Each module is my analysis of a book on an entrepreneur's life. Stand Up is not affiliated with or endorsed by the authors or publishers. The books are the authors' work; I recommend reading them. This is my own commentary, not a summary or replacement for the book. Education, not advice.
public_title: Conviction, Accountability and Where to Draw the Line
public_outcome: My reading of one book about an entrepreneur's life, in the book's order. We look at getting lost in a goal, crisis, smart money and dumb money, where the line is, approval and accountability, and time and priorities. Built from my group calls.
